I’ve been farming these lands in Quzhou County for over thirty years, and I know what works here on the North China Plain. The soil is good, the water table is manageable if we irrigate properly, and the buyers always come for wheat and maize. I don’t chase risky crops — I grow what feeds my family and what I can sell at the grain station without worry.

This year, I will stick to the rotation every household around here trusts: winter wheat followed by summer maize. It’s the only way to get two crops off the same piece of land and still have time to rest the soil. I’ve got 8 mu in total, and I’ll split them evenly — though in this system, it’s really the same 8 mu planted twice. I use improved wheat seeds because they resist lodging better than the old varieties, and hybrid maize because it gives me the highest yield in the short summer window.

For wheat, I’ll rotary till the field before sowing in early October, apply compound fertilizer as basal dressing, and top-dress with urea in spring. I’ll irrigate three times: once at green-up, once at heading, and once at grain filling. I spray for weeds, aphids, and fungus about four times in total.

For maize, I plant it right after the wheat harvest in early June — no need to plough deeply, I just no-till sow into the wheat stubble. Maize needs less fertilizer than wheat but more water in July heat, so I’ll irrigate twice. I spray herbicide and insecticide about three times to keep armyworms and weeds down.

I expect about 1,000 jin per mu for wheat and about 1,100 jin per mu for maize. That’s what my neighbors and I usually get when the weather cooperates.
